从入学说明会到毕业谢恩会，跟着留学生リン走完四年：交朋友、请教老师、社团、发表与: From orientation for new students to the graduation thank-you party for the faculty, follow international student Lin through four years of university: making friends, asking professors for help, joining a club, giving presentations and writing a thesis, and learning to earn people's trust at a Japanese university.
四月初，大学礼堂里正在开新生入学说明会。リン到得有点晚，前排都坐满了，只有日本女: It's early April, and the orientation for new students is underway in the university auditorium. Lin has arrived a little late. The front rows are all full, and the only empty seat left is next to a Japanese student, Yui Sato. The course registration handbook in her hands is packed with tiny writing. Lin works up her courage, walks over, and speaks up.
经济学部一年级日本学生，静冈人，开朗爱笑: First-year Japanese student in the Faculty of Economics, from Shizuoka; cheerful and always smiling
中国留学生，经济学部一年级，刚到日本两周: International student from China, first year in the Faculty of Economics; arrived in Japan just two weeks ago
两人同年级、第一次见面。日本同学之间初次见面也会先用「です・ます」的丁宁体，等对: They're in the same year and meeting for the first time. Even between Japanese students, a first meeting starts in the polite 「です・ます」 style, and they only switch naturally to the plain style after one of them says something like "just call me by my first name." This lesson shows exactly that moment of shifting from polite to close.
不好意思，这里有人吗？: Excuse me, is this seat free?
在教室、电车里问座位，最常用的就是「空いていますか」。直接说「座ってもいいですか: When asking about a seat in a classroom or on a train, the most common phrase is 「空いていますか」. You could also say 「座ってもいいですか」 directly, but checking first whether anyone is sitting there is more considerate: if the seat is being saved for a friend, it's easy for the other person to say so.
谢谢。我是经济学部的林，从中国来的。: Thank you. I'm Lin, in the Faculty of Economics. I'm from China.
日本大学里自我介绍，习惯先报学部（院系），再说名字。对同年级同学用「〜です」刚刚: When introducing yourself at a Japanese university, it's customary to give your 「学部」 (faculty or department) first, then your name. With classmates in the same year, 「〜です」 is just right; 「〜と申します」 would sound like a job interview and make the other person feel distance.
我也是经济学部的！我叫佐藤由衣，请多关照。: I'm in the Faculty of Economics too! I'm Yui Sato. Nice to meet you.
请多关照。佐藤同学是哪里人？: Nice to meet you too. Where are you from, Sato?
静冈。是个以茶出名的地方。林同学是中国哪里的？: Shizuoka. It's a place famous for its tea. Where in China are you from, Lin?
成都。以熊猫和辣菜出名。: Chengdu. It's famous for pandas and spicy food.
哇，真好。你喜欢吃辣的吗？: Wow, that sounds great. So do you like spicy food?
超喜欢。那个……这个选课的说明，有点难懂……: I love it. Um, this explanation of course registration is kind of hard to follow…
「〜て……」把话说一半停下来，是日语里很常见的求助方式：不直接说「教えてください: 「〜て……」, stopping halfway through a sentence, is a very common way to ask for help in Japanese. Instead of saying 「教えてください」 outright, you let the sentence trail off, and the other person will naturally pick it up with something like 「一緒に見ましょうか」. It's softer than a direct request and leaves the other person some room.
我懂。我也看不太明白。待会儿要不要一起去教务处问问？: I know what you mean. I don't really get it either. Would you like to go ask at the office together later?
那我们交换一下联系方式吧？: Then why don't we exchange contact info?
好。那个……我可以叫你「由衣」吗？: Sure. Um, is it okay if I call you "Yui-san"?
日本人对称呼很敏感，直接叫名字（下の名前）算是拉近一步。先问一句「呼んでもいいで: Japanese people are quite sensitive about how they're addressed, and calling someone by their first name (「下の名前」) is a step closer. If you ask 「呼んでもいいですか」 first, the other person will feel that you're tactful, and she'll be happy that you want to be friends.
当然。叫我「由衣」就行啦。我也叫你「小林」哦。: Of course. Just "Yui" is fine. And I'll call you "Lin-chan."
注意这里ゆい的语气一下子从「です・ます」变成了「いいよ」「呼ぶね」。这是她在表示: Notice how Yui's tone suddenly shifts here from 「です・ます」 to 「いいよ」 and 「呼ぶね」. This is her way of saying "we're friends now." At this point you can relax too and answer in the plain style; sticking with polite speech would actually come across as rejecting her friendliness.
「経済学部」「文学部」。自我介绍先说「〜学部の〜です」: 「経済学部」 (Faculty of Economics), 「文学部」 (Faculty of Letters). When introducing yourself, start with 「〜学部の〜です」
出生地、老家；毕业学校: hometown, place of origin; school one graduated from
「ご出身はどちらですか」是礼貌地问对方老家，初次见面的万能话题: 「ご出身はどちらですか」 is a polite way to ask where someone is from, a go-to topic when meeting someone for the first time
「履修登録」= 选课登记；「履修する」= 修这门课: 「履修登録」 = course registration; 「履修する」 = to take a course
「入学説明会」「就職説明会」，开学和找工作都会遇到: 「入学説明会」 (orientation for new students), 「就職説明会」 (recruiting information session): you'll come across these both when starting university and when job hunting
（座位、时间）空着: to be free, to be vacant (seat, time)
「席が空いている」「明日空いてる？」= 明天有空吗: 「席が空いている」 (the seat is free); 「明日空いてる？」 = Are you free tomorrow?
「隣の席」= 旁边的座位，「隣の人」= 邻座的人或邻居: 「隣の席」 = the seat next to you; 「隣の人」 = the person next to you, or the neighbor
「〜で有名だ」= 因……而出名，介绍家乡时很好用: 「〜で有名だ」 = famous for ...; handy when introducing your hometown
大学里办手续、问事情的地方，也常叫「事務」「窓口」: The place at a university where you do paperwork and ask questions; also often called 「事務」 or 「窓口」
「連絡先を交換する」= 交换联系方式，现在多指加 LINE: 「連絡先を交換する」 = to exchange contact information; these days it usually means adding each other on LINE
「連絡先の交換」「意見交換」= 交流意见: 「連絡先の交換」 (exchanging contact info); 「意見交換」 = exchanging opinions
称呼；叫来: to call (by a name); to call (someone over)
「〜って呼んで」= 叫我……就行，用来拉近关系: 「〜って呼んで」 = just call me ...; used to get closer to someone
动词て形 + もいいですか: Verb て-form + もいいですか
把决定权交给对方，是最基础的礼貌问法。对同学用「〜てもいい？」，对老师、长辈要升: It leaves the decision to the other person, making it the most basic polite way to ask. With classmates use 「〜てもいい？」; with professors and elders, step it up to 「〜てもよろしいでしょうか」. In Japan, asking first, even about something small, makes people feel respected.
可以叫你名字吗？: Is it okay if I call you by your first name?
一緒に + 动词ます形去ます + ませんか: 一緒に + verb ます-stem + ませんか
用否定疑问来邀请，意思是「如果你愿意的话」，对方不想去也好拒绝。比「〜しましょう: Inviting with a negative question carries the sense of "if you'd like to," so it's easy for the other person to decline if they don't want to go. It's more polite than 「〜しましょう」 and suits people you've just met. Once you're close, it becomes 「一緒に行かない？」.
要不要一起吃午饭？: Would you like to have lunch together?
要不要一起去图书馆？: Would you like to go to the library together?
开学典礼、说明会、第一堂课、社团活动这些大家都还不认识的场合，主动问座位、报学部: At the entrance ceremony, orientation, the first class, club activities, and any other occasion where nobody knows each other yet, taking the initiative to ask about a seat and give your faculty and name is the most natural way to start. That's how Japanese students get to know each other too.
很多中国同学一紧张就用「〜と申します」「〜でございます」，对同学太重了；也有人一: When they get nervous, many learners slip into 「〜と申します」 or 「〜でございます」, which is far too heavy with classmates. Others jump straight into the plain style or call someone by their first name without waiting for the other person's OK, which can come across as a bit forward.
日本学生其实也很想交朋友，只是不太好意思先开口。你先说一句「空いていますか」，对: Japanese students actually want to make friends too; they're just too shy to speak first. If you start with 「空いていますか」, the other person will feel relieved: "Great, someone came over to talk to me." And that little bit of care when you ask how to address her will make her feel you're someone she can trust.
日本人第一次见面不太会热情地问东问西，很多留学生会觉得「日本人好冷淡」。其实大多: At a first meeting, Japanese people don't usually pepper you with eager questions, and many international students come away thinking "Japanese people are so cold." In fact, most are just shy and waiting for a chance to speak up. So don't be afraid of making mistakes: be brave, say 「すみません」 first, and things will get started. One more small thing matters a lot: remember the other person's name from your first meeting, and the next time you see them, say 「ゆいさん、おはよう」. Japanese people feel valued because "you remembered me," and that is often where trust begins. Taking care to remember a name touches people more than any number of beautiful sentences.
在教室里看到一个空位，旁边坐着不认识的同学，最自然的说法是？: You see an empty seat in a classroom, next to a classmate you don't know. What's the most natural thing to say?
对陌生同学用丁宁体问「空いていますか」最自然。第二、四个太随便，第三个敬语过头，: With a classmate you don't know, asking 「空いていますか」 in the polite style is the most natural. The second and fourth are too casual, and the third is over-the-top keigo, like something out of a period drama.
初次见面跟同年级同学自我介绍，哪个最合适？: You're introducing yourself to a classmate in your year for the first time. Which is the most appropriate?
同学之间用「〜です」加「よろしくお願いします」刚好。过度敬语会显得生分，普通体又: Between classmates, 「〜です」 plus 「よろしくお願いします」 is just right. Excessive keigo sounds distant, and the plain style is too soon.
对方说「『ゆい』でいいよ」，这句话背后的意思是？: When the other person says 「『ゆい』でいいよ」, what does she really mean?
她不想被叫名字: She doesn't want to be called by her name
她希望你用更正式的敬语: She wants you to use more formal keigo
她愿意跟你更亲近，可以用名字和普通体: She's happy to get closer to you, so you can use her first name and the plain style
允许你直接叫名字，又用了普通体，是在表示「我们是朋友了」。你也可以跟着放松语气。: Letting you call her by her first name, and using the plain style herself, is her way of saying "we're friends now." You can relax your tone too.
